content_html:
A required minimum distribution (RMD) is the smallest amount the IRS requires you to withdraw each year from a traditional IRA, SEP IRA, SIMPLE IRA, 401(k), 403(b) or most 457(b) plans once you reach your RMD starting age. This calculator finds your RMD for a given year from your account balance and age, and projects the RMDs that follow.

How to use this calculator

  1. Year of birth: sets your RMD starting age and your age in the distribution year.
  2. Distribution year: the year you want the RMD for.
  3. Account balance: the account's value on December 31 of the year before the distribution year, as shown on your year-end statement.
  4. Expected annual return: used only to project future balances and RMDs, not for the RMD of the year you chose.

When RMDs start

The SECURE Act and the SECURE 2.0 Act raised the starting age based on when you were born:

Year of birthRMD starting age
Before July 1, 194970½
July 1, 1949 to 195072
1951 to 195973
1960 or later75

Your first RMD is for the year you reach that age, and you can delay it until April 1 of the following year. Every later RMD is due by December 31. Delaying the first one means taking two RMDs in the same year, which can push you into a higher tax bracket. If you are still working, a 401(k) at your current employer usually lets you wait until you retire, unless you own more than 5% of the company. Roth IRAs have no RMDs while the owner is alive, and since 2024 neither do Roth 401(k) accounts.

How the RMD is calculated

Divide the prior December 31 balance by the distribution period from the IRS Uniform Lifetime Table for the age you reach by the end of the distribution year. The table, in IRS Publication 590-B, has been in effect since 2022. Some values:

AgeDistribution periodShare of balance
7326.53.77%
7524.64.07%
8020.24.95%
8516.06.25%
9012.28.20%
958.911.24%

If your spouse is the sole beneficiary of the account for the whole year and is more than 10 years younger than you, the IRS Joint and Last Survivor Table applies instead. It gives a longer distribution period and a smaller RMD than this calculator shows.

Worked example

Someone born in 1952 reached their RMD starting age of 73 in 2025. In 2026 they turn 74, and their IRA was worth $300,000 on December 31, 2025. The distribution period for age 74 is 25.5, so the 2026 RMD is $300,000 ÷ 25.5 = $11,764.71, due by December 31, 2026. If the account earns 5% a year and they withdraw only the RMD, the projection shows about $12,326.64 for 2027 and $12,914.36 for 2028. RMDs tend to rise because the divisor shrinks each year.

Practical tips

  • Calculate the RMD separately for each account. IRA RMDs can be totaled and taken from any one or more of your IRAs, and 403(b) RMDs work the same way among 403(b)s, but each 401(k) must pay out its own RMD.
  • You can always withdraw more than the minimum, but extra withdrawals don't count toward future years' RMDs.
  • A missed RMD triggers a 25% excise tax on the amount not taken, reduced to 10% if it is corrected in time.
  • From age 70½, a qualified charitable distribution from an IRA can count toward your RMD without being added to taxable income.
  • Inherited accounts follow different rules. Use a beneficiary RMD calculator for those.

faq.question: When is the deadline for taking my RMD?
faq.answer: December 31 of each distribution year. The only exception is your first RMD, which can be delayed until April 1 of the following year. If you delay it, you must also take your second RMD by December 31 of that same year.

faq.question: Which balance do I use to calculate my RMD?
faq.answer: Use the account's fair market value on December 31 of the year before the distribution year. Changes in value during the distribution year don't affect that year's RMD.

faq.question: Are RMDs taxed?
faq.answer: Withdrawals from traditional pre-tax accounts are taxed as ordinary income in the year you take them. Any after-tax money you contributed comes out tax-free. Many custodians let you have federal tax withheld from the distribution.

faq.question: Do I have to take an RMD from a Roth IRA?
faq.answer: No. Roth IRA owners never have to take RMDs, and since 2024 the same is true of Roth 401(k) and Roth 403(b) accounts. Beneficiaries who inherit a Roth account do have distribution requirements.

faq.question: What if I am still working at my RMD starting age?
faq.answer: Many employer plans let you delay RMDs from your current employer's plan until April 1 of the year after you retire, as long as you don't own more than 5% of the business. This doesn't apply to IRAs or to plans from former employers.
